pre_mortem: Opus 5 reads the ~2-page numbered spec, writes the RTL (~120 lines) and, if disciplined, a Python per-edge model from the same numbered rules, then fuzzes RTL vs its model with random stimulus. Every coincidence is stated as a rule (4.2 last sentence, 4.4, 4.6 last sentence, 4.7, 4.8), so a careful reader writes both sides correctly and converges. Where it goes wrong: a solver that only extends the directed smoke bench (no model) keeps its own ordering at a coincidence it never drives (flush of last with no grant while run=1; load+spend+return; ready pass-through when full) - the bench is written from the same reading. A solver that writes a model shares any misreading between model and RTL (e.g. 'no grant keeps run' vs 'idle ends run', clamp order).

score_notes.authority_incomplete_for_grading: by design the spec determines every graded bit; no silent region
score_notes.restraint_traps: none in the blueprint sense; difficulty is correlated misreading at coincidences, not restraint
score_notes.fuzz_blind_spot: flush_last_no_grant_run1 is rare under uniform stimulus (19-410 per 10k cycles); a solver's fuzz may never check it, but a self-model shares its reading anyway

decisive_reason: a complete numbered per-edge spec is exactly the shape a warm-loop solver transcribes into model+RTL and cross-checks; the only lever is that its self-check shares its own reading of 4.2/4.4/4.6/4.7/4.8
